body: Do waves have this seam?  Maybe we can make use of that seam to deliver in a Wave's final guardrails or tasks?

Yes — and this is better than what I designed. Verified three things rather than guessing:

1. WaveJournalEntry.Exit already IS the per-wave gate I was inventing as <plan>/deliveryGates/<group>/ — a full PlanGuardrailsSection, 'the plan-guardrail phase scoped to this wave, always re-evaluated on the current HEAD' (SSOT 14.6).
2. Scheduler.cs:1144 DeliverAndCleanup is already 'shared by the flat and waved paths' — the mergeOnSuccess machinery is factored, it just fires once at run end.
3. Wave ordering is strict, so 'the docs sink delivers last' is just 'put the sink in the last wave'. My deliverAfter field disappears entirely.

So #525 collapses from 'invent deliveryGroups + per-group gates + delivery ordering' to 'fire the existing delivery at each wave's existing exit gate'. Most of my sections 1-3 stop being needed.

The one real cost, and it is a doctrine change rather than a detail: plan-breakdown currently says 'Do NOT wave a flat plan — a wave barrier destroys cross-wave parallelism' (SSOT 14 C5). Plan 25's three chains are INDEPENDENT and could run in parallel; three waves serialises them. A wave still holds a parallel task DAG internally, so what you lose is parallelism ACROSS issues, not within one.

Your idea therefore adds a SECOND legitimate reason to wave — delivery granularity — alongside the existing one (stages whose downstream tasks cannot be authored until the upstream is real). That is your call, so I am rewriting the design around the wave seam and raising the parallelism trade as its own question rather than deciding it.
I'm willing to live with the wave limitation of only running serially, as syncing to master and merging them in, leans us toward serial working for our worktree/branches anyhow.

body: So, a delivery in this case isn't required for each wave.  It may be that 2 GH issues that are being solved both require a change to common code (maybe a DTO, etc) and it may be that the changes need to be done in a wave, but that it isn't required that they make it into a PR before either one of the issues are implemented (of course depending on which order the wave of each GH issue placed).

Agreed, and this breaks an assumption I had not noticed I was making: draft 2 treats EVERY wave as a delivery unit. Your DTO case shows why that is wrong — a shared-prerequisite wave has no standalone value as a PR, and delivering it alone would put a DTO change on your branch with no consumer.

So delivery has to be a property of SOME waves, not all, and it decouples cleanly from ordering:

  wave-01-shared-dto    delivers: false   (prerequisite; nothing to ship on its own)
  wave-02-issue-510     delivers: true    -> merges waves 01 + 02 together
  wave-03-issue-511     delivers: true    -> merges wave 03

A delivering wave ships everything ACCUMULATED SINCE THE LAST DELIVERY POINT, so a non-delivering wave simply rides along with the next one that does. The plan branch already accumulates exactly that way, so this needs no new mechanism — just a per-wave flag and a 'since last delivery point' notion of what the merge covers.

That also replaces my plan-level deliverPerWave bool, which was the wrong grain: it forced all-or-nothing on a plan whose whole point is that its waves differ. Per-wave 'delivers' (default false) keeps the never-weaker guarantee AND expresses your case directly.

It sharpens the gate question too. The gate that matters is the DELIVERING wave's exit gate, evaluated over the accumulated tree — which is what the plan branch already holds at that barrier, so the prerequisite wave's code is under test at the moment it ships rather than when it was written.

Revising now; the opt-in question is being reworded from a plan-level bool to the per-wave flag.
If plan-level preflights are deterministically required, then a wave after a delivery wave, should also follow this requirement.

anchor.quote: a wave barrier destroys cross-wave parallelism

body: Are you arguing for cross-wave parallelism?  Seems like it adds complications to the design, more potential race conditions and makes it harder to represent in the task table as well as in a mermaid diagram of the live status.  Right?

No — the opposite, and the anchor is misleading because it is a QUOTE, not my argument.

That sentence is plan-breakdown's OWN rule, block-quoted in §2 so the cost of this design's doctrine change can be named against it. The full quote is 'Do NOT wave a flat plan — fine-grained parallelism is a task DAG inside ONE wave, not multiple waves ... a wave barrier destroys cross-wave parallelism'. §2 then says what that costs HERE: plan 25's three chains are independent and can run in parallel today, so putting them in three waves to get per-wave delivery SERIALISES them, and that is a real loss.

So the barrier is a feature I am keeping, not a limitation I am arguing to remove. Your three objections are exactly why: more race surface, a task table that no longer reads as a DAG, and a live-status mermaid that cannot show what is actually running. I would add a fourth — cross-wave parallelism would break the one property the barrier buys, which is that a wave's exit gate runs on a quiescent tree. There is no such moment if a later wave is already mid-flight.

And you have already settled this. On 7 Sept you replied: 'I'm willing to live with the wave limitation of only running serially, as syncing to master and merging them in, leans us toward serial working for our worktree/branches anyhow.'

That is the decision, and the gap is mine: it lives only in this review log, not in the design. §2 currently names the cost and stops, so a later reader meets the loss with no record that it was weighed and accepted. Folding it in as a DECIDED marker with your reasoning — that the sync-and-merge model leans serial anyway, so the parallelism being given up is less than it looks on paper.

Agreed on the principle, and I have to correct the premise — checked rather than assumed, because it changes what the answer costs.

THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD TODAY. Plan-level preflights are NOT deterministically required. I grepped DiagnosticCodes.cs: nothing requires a preflight to EXIST. GR2027 is about a malformed 'catches:' line in any of the four folders, and GR2028 requires a multi-leaf plan's TERMINAL gate to carry a real integration re-run. The #181 positive baseline is a plan-breakdown authoring rule with a worth-it gate — emitted when the plan is brownfield and the gate passes, skipped with a stated reason otherwise. No validate check fires if it is missing.

So 'follow the same requirement' currently means 'be an authoring rule too', which is what §1c already says — and that is the weaker reading of your comment.

THE STRONGER READING IS THE RIGHT ONE, AND IT IS A REAL GAP. An instruction with no gate behind it is this repo's most-repeated defect shape, and §1c is currently exactly that: 'plan-breakdown emits a positive-baseline entry preflight for every post-delivery wave', enforced by nobody. You answered d39-positive-baseline-at-wave-entry with 'Yes — plan-breakdown emits one for every post-delivery wave', so the authoring rule is settled; what your comment adds is whether it should also be CERTIFIED.

I think it should, and that it justifies holding a wave to a HIGHER bar than the plan level, which is the part worth arguing with. The blast radii differ:

  a missing PLAN-level baseline    the run attributes a pre-existing failure to the first
                                   task that touches the area. Slow and annoying, on a run
                                   you are typically watching.
  a missing POST-DELIVERY wave     the wave builds on a tree a refresh just changed, and the
  baseline                         failure surfaces at that wave's EXIT gate — blaming a wave
                                   that did nothing wrong. That is the attribution defect §1c
                                   exists to prevent, reappearing because the control meant
                                   to prevent it was optional.

Next free is GR2078 (GR2077 is reserved by #587 check B). Adding this as a fourth question rather than deciding it, because 'a new ERROR code' is a real cost — it fails plans that are correct-but-unguarded, and you may prefer the WARNING that names the gap without blocking.
